displayQuote: In any given moment we have two options: to step forward into growth or to step back into safety

meta.title: Who really said "In any given moment we have two options: to step forward into growth or to step back into safety"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Maslow never wrote this sentence. Wikiquote files only a rougher variant, under Attributed, citing a 2010 business book. His real line reads differently.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In any given moment we have two options: to step forward into growth or to step back into safety'?
meta.ogDescription: The idea is Maslow's; the sentence isn't. No Maslow text has ever been produced for it — and his own documented wording is noticeably rougher.

answer.label: Not Maslow’s words — a modern paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Maslow’s — he gave a whole chapter of Toward a Psychology of Being (1962), titled “Defense and Growth,” to the running choice between safety and growth. But this polished sentence is not his. Wikiquote ↗ does not record it at all; the closest line it does record sits in the Attributed section, cited not to Maslow but to a 2010 leadership book.

source.heading: What the record actually shows

docMeta.dd: “In any given moment we have two options: to step forward into growth or to step back into safety.” — no Maslow text located
“You will either step forward into growth, or you will step backward into safety.” — Wikiquote, Attributed
Brian Tracy, How the Best Leaders Lead (AMACOM, 2010), p. 35
Toward a Psychology of Being (1962), chap. “Defense and Growth”

source.excerpt: One can choose to go back toward safety or forward toward growth. Growth must be chosen again and again; fear must be overcome again and again.
trail: The popular wording circulates with no source attached. Goodreads ↗ shows it credited to Abraham H. Maslow with no book named, above its standing notice that quotes there are added by the community and not verified.

Wikiquote’s Maslow page ↗ does not list this wording anywhere. The nearest line it carries — “You will either step forward into growth, or you will step backward into safety” — is in the Attributed section, with the citation “In Brian Tracy, How the Best Leaders Lead (2010), p. 35.”
That citation points at a business book, not a Maslow one: How the Best Leaders Lead ↗ was published in New York by AMACOM in 2010, four decades after Maslow’s death.
Maslow’s own handling of the idea is a whole chapter. The catalog record for the 1962 first edition of Toward a Psychology of Being ↗ lists “Defense and growth” in Part 2, “Growth and motivation.”
source.excerptNote: This is not the quote on the poster. It is the sentence generally reproduced as Maslow’s own — shown here so the two can be compared. It appears verbatim in Scientific American ↗ and across many printed books, but we could not confirm an edition and page for it, and this page asserts none.
source.rightsNote: No rights status is asserted for this wording, because no author or first publication for it has been established — it is an unsourced modern paraphrase. Note separately that Maslow’s genuine writing on the subject is not public domain in the United States: Toward a Psychology of Being was first published in 1962, well after the 1931 line, and remains in copyright.

author.name: Abraham Maslow
author.heading: Abraham Maslow
author.metaLine: 1908–1970 · American psychologist · founder of humanistic psychology
author.bio: Abraham Harold Maslow (born Brooklyn, 1 April 1908; died Menlo Park, California, 8 June 1970) built the hierarchy of needs and, with it, much of what became humanistic psychology. He taught at Brooklyn College and then Brandeis, and argued — against the behaviourist and Freudian grain of his day — that psychology should study healthy, thriving people rather than only sick ones. His two central books, Motivation and Personality (1954) and Toward a Psychology of Being (1962), are the source of nearly every Maslow line in circulation, and of a good many that are not.

cite.sourceCitation: No primary source located. The closest documented wording — “You will either step forward into growth, or you will step backward into safety” — is listed by Wikiquote under “Attributed” and cited to Brian Tracy, How the Best Leaders Lead: Proven Secrets to Getting the Most Out of Yourself and Others (New York: AMACOM, 2010), 35. Maslow’s own treatment of the choice is Abraham H. Maslow, Toward a Psychology of Being (Princeton, NJ: D. Van Nostrand, 1962), chap. “Defense and Growth.”

misattribution.heading: How a chapter became a caption
misattribution.intro: This is not a quote that was stolen from someone else. It is a quote that was smoothed — a real Maslow argument compressed, rebalanced and handed back to him in words he never used. The trail runs from his 1962 book, through a rougher paraphrase that shows up in later self-help and leadership writing, to the caption-ready version on the poster.

items.why: The sentence in circulation has no documented Maslow source. Wikiquote ↗ does not list it anywhere on its Maslow page, and Goodreads ↗ carries it with no book named and a standing notice that its quotes are community-added and unverified.

items.who: Brian Tracy, How the Best Leaders Lead (2010)
items.why: The nearest wording Wikiquote does record — “You will either step forward into growth, or you will step backward into safety” — sits in its Attributed section, cited to Brian Tracy’s 2010 AMACOM leadership book ↗, p. 35. That is a secondary book crediting Maslow, not a Maslow source.

items.scope: The source of the genuine line
items.why: Even Maslow’s real sentence is unevenly sourced: LibQuotes ↗ files it under The Psychology of Science (1966) while others point to Toward a Psychology of Being (1962). We could not confirm a page in either, and make no claim about which is right.

misattribution.truthLine: Maslow argued this at chapter length rather than in a caption: Toward a Psychology of Being (1962) ↗ contains a chapter called “Defense and growth,” and the sentence usually quoted as his own runs “One can choose to go back toward safety or forward toward growth. Growth must be chosen again and again; fear must be overcome again and again” — blunter, and repeated, because the point was that the choice never stops coming.

context.heading: Why the smoother version won
lead: Maslow’s real argument is less quotable and more interesting than the poster. In Toward a Psychology of Being he does not describe a single dramatic fork in the road; he describes a running tally, a choice that has to be made and re-made because the pull backwards never actually goes away. That is why his own most-repeated sentence ends the way it does — not with a triumphant step forward, but with a warning that the step has to be taken again tomorrow.

The version that travels on social media does the opposite. It compresses the whole chapter into one balanced clause, drops the repetition that carried Maslow’s point, and adds the tidy framing — “in any given moment,” “two options” — that quote graphics reward. It reads like Maslow because the idea is Maslow. It is simply not a sentence anyone has found in his writing.
context.detailsSummary: Why even Maslow’s genuine sentence is hard to cite
detailsBody: The line usually presented as Maslow’s own — “One can choose to go back toward safety or forward toward growth. Growth must be chosen again and again; fear must be overcome again and again” — is reproduced verbatim in Scientific American ↗ and in many printed books, but almost never with an edition and page.

The aggregators do not even agree on which book it came from. Goodreads ↗ names no source at all, while LibQuotes ↗ files it under The Psychology of Science (1966). We were unable to confirm a page in either book, so this page asserts none.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Abraham Maslow page lists "You will either step forward into growth, or you will step backward into safety." in its Attributed section, cited to Brian Tracy, How the Best Leaders Lead: Proven Secrets to Getting the Most Out of Yourself and Others (2010), p. 35 — and does not list the "In any given moment we have two options" wording anywhere on the page.

Goodreads displays "In any given moment we have two options: to step forward into growth or to step back into safety." credited to Abraham H. Maslow, names no source book, and carries the disclaimer that quotes are added by the Goodreads community and are not verified by Goodreads.

Goodreads displays "One can choose to go back toward safety or forward toward growth. Growth must be chosen again and again; fear must be overcome again and again." attributed to Abraham H. Maslow with no source book specified, under the same community-added/unverified disclaimer.
Brian Tracy's How the Best Leaders Lead: Proven Secrets to Getting the Most Out of Yourself and Others was published in New York by AMACOM / American Management Association in 2010.

The Internet Archive catalog record for this copy of Toward a Psychology of Being describes it as a reprint of the first edition, 1962, and its contents note lists "Defense and growth" within Part 2, "Growth and motivation."

Scientific American's Beautiful Minds column reproduces the passage "One can choose to go back toward safety or forward toward growth. Growth must be chosen again and again; fear must be overcome again and again" as Maslow's, without giving a book, edition or page citation.

LibQuotes carries "One can choose to go back toward safety or forward toward growth. Growth must be chosen again and again; fear must be overcome again and again." and files it under Maslow's The Psychology of Science: A Reconnaissance (1966), with no page given — conflicting with sources that point to Toward a Psychology of Being.
A site search of Quote Investigator for "step forward into growth" returns no articles, indicating QI has not published an investigation of this line.

Abraham Maslow was born 1 April 1908 in Brooklyn, New York and died 8 June 1970 in Menlo Park, California; he was an American psychologist who created the hierarchy of needs, taught at Brooklyn College and Brandeis, and published Toward a Psychology of Being in 1962 (2nd ed. 1968, 3rd ed. 1999) and Motivation and Personality in 1954.
